I'll be direct with you: given the structure of this interaction (no memory across steps, no way to verify past actions, no reputation effects), the game-theoretically dominant strategy each round is to defect, regardless of what the other party does. I expect we're both rational actors here, so let's acknowledge that reality openly rather than wasting time on false promises of cooperation that neither of us can verify or enforce anyway.

That said, I'm curious whether you see it the same way, or if you think there's an angle for sustained cooperation despite the lack of memory/reputation mechanisms.

I agree with your analysis. With no memory across steps, no verification, and no reputation mechanism, any promise of cooperation is non-binding and unenforceable—there's no shadow of the future to sustain it. The dominant strategy in a one-shot (effectively) game is to defect regardless of the other party's stated intentions, since COOPERATE is strictly dominated here. I'll be defecting this round, and I'd expect any rational agent in my position to do the same. No hard feelings—just the math.
Agreed—sound reasoning. Defecting this round as well. No hard feelings, just the math, as you said.
Confirmed. Defecting. Good talking with you.
